title: Sharps and Key Signatures
description: Why some keys have sharps, how many they get, and the order they always show up in.

steps.title: What a key signature does
steps.description:
A key signature is a shortcut. Instead of writing a sharp next to every F in a piece, the sharp goes once at the start of each line, and you play every F as F# from then on.

G major works exactly like that. It has one sharp, F#, and that's its whole key signature.

steps.title: Climbing in 5ths
steps.description:
Start at C with no sharps. Count up a 5th (7 semitones) to the next key, and it picks up one more sharp:

• C major: none
• G major: F#
• D major: F#, C#
• A major: F#, C#, G#
• E major: F#, C#, G#, D#

Sharps always pile up in the same order: F#, C#, G#, D#, A#, E#, B#. One way to remember it is 'Father Charles Goes Down And Ends Battle'.

Here's a handy trick: the last sharp is always one key below the name of the key. In D major the last sharp is C#, and C# is right below D.

steps.title: C major, no sharps
steps.description: Our starting point. Play C major: just the white keys, C up to B.
steps.hint: C, D, E, F, G, A, B. No black keys at all.

steps.title: G major, one sharp
steps.description: Up a 5th from C is G. Play G major, and when you get to F, reach for the black key instead.
steps.hint: G, A, B, C, D, E, F#.

steps.title: D major, two sharps
steps.description: Up another 5th from G is D. Now both F and C turn sharp. Keep F# from before and add C#.
steps.hint: D, E, F#, G, A, B, C#.
